title: Knowledge check — 8 questions
note: Unlocks after the applied activity is submitted. Retakes are free and unlimited.

questions.prompt: What makes zero-result search logs higher-fidelity than a survey?
options: They have a larger sample size
They are unprompted and behavioural — someone needed something enough to type it, and it isn't shaped by a question you thought to ask
They are easier to analyze with AI
They are anonymous by default
questions.explanation: A survey measures response to your question, so it is blind wherever your assumptions are. Search measures what someone needed unbidden, and typing a query is a costly signal, only worth it if you actually need the answer.

questions.prompt: Why is thematic synthesis particularly prone to false confidence?
options: Models are trained mostly on formal writing
Because there is no natural failure signal — no equivalent of a checkable fabricated citation — so the output looks identical whether the structure is real or imposed
Because themes are inherently subjective
Because ticket data is usually incomplete
questions.explanation: Ask for four hundred tickets to be themed and you'll get themes, whether or not themes exist. The three cheap defences: ask for the distribution, ask what didn't fit and how much, and run it twice to see whether the structure holds.

questions.prompt: How does re-identification differ from the small-sample problem?
options: It only applies to qualitative data
It affects large organizations rather than small ones
The analysis can be perfectly sound — the problem is that the output identifies people against a promise you made, so the fix is a reporting floor rather than a confidence interval
It is a statistical error rather than a disclosure
questions.explanation: "Three of five raised concerns about their manager" may be entirely accurate. It is also a disclosure, and the manager reading it knows who the silent two probably are.

questions.prompt: What does the EU AI Act's workplace emotion-recognition prohibition actually cover `[V]`?
options: Any AI system that infers employee sentiment, including from text
Inference from biometric data — so a camera reading faces in a town hall is prohibited, while text sentiment analysis very probably falls outside it
Only systems used in performance management decisions
Nothing yet; the obligations begin in 2027
questions.explanation: The prohibition's text doesn't say "biometric," but Commission guidance ties it to the Act's defined term, which is limited to inference from biometric data. In force since 2 February 2025 and absolute, with narrow medical and safety exceptions.

questions.prompt: What is the practical consequence of "not prohibited isn't cleared"?
options: That legal review is unnecessary where no prohibition applies
That escaping Article 5 clears one gate of at least four — data protection, works councils, monitoring notice, and §7 all still apply
That organizations should apply the strictest jurisdiction's rules everywhere
That prohibitions are less important than guidance
questions.explanation: And it cuts the other way too: "we can't, it's illegal in the EU" isn't available as a reason for text analysis, so anyone who has been using it has been winning an argument on a premise that won't survive the first person who checks.

questions.prompt: New York, Connecticut and Delaware require what, precisely `[V]`?
options: Employee consent before any electronic monitoring
Notice — written or electronic, with acknowledgment and in some cases conspicuous posting. They do not prohibit monitoring; they require you to have said you were doing it
Annual reporting of monitoring activity to the state
A documented impact assessment before monitoring begins
questions.explanation: Which turns the question into a specific, answerable one: does the notice your employees actually acknowledged cover what you're proposing to build? A 2019 notice about telephone, email and internet usage isn't obviously notice of sentiment inference across internal chat.

questions.prompt: GC 23-02 on electronic surveillance was rescinded in February 2025 `[V]`. What should a listening programme conclude?
options: That electronic monitoring is now permitted under the NLRA
That §7 no longer applies to algorithmic management
That the statute and the Board's decisional law are unchanged — only the enforcement appetite of one office moved, and a programme designed against posture breaks when posture flips
That the rescission will likely be reversed, so the memo should still be followed
questions.explanation: A team that built its rules around the memo now has rules with no foundation. A team that built them around "don't build systems that would tend to chill protected concerted activity" has rules exactly as valid as before, and still valid when the posture flips back.

questions.prompt: What is the strongest argument *against* the promise-based rule?
options: That employees do not read privacy notices, so the promise has no effect

That it systematically protects the powerful — the patterns suppressed by a reporting floor are concentrated in small teams, which is exactly where a bad manager's effects show up, among the people least able to escalate
That anonymity cannot be guaranteed in any dataset
That competitors who analyze freely will gain an advantage
questions.explanation: A floor set at five may be protecting the manager rather than the five. That is why the activity asks what you'd actually do with a small-team signal suggesting harm — "the floor forbids it" is a policy, not an answer, and every listening programme eventually meets this case.
